title: Four Types of Sentences
keyIdea: Every sentence has a job, and its job gives its type. A statement tells you something and ends with a full stop. A question asks something and ends with a question mark. An exclamation shows a big feeling; it starts with What or How, has a verb, and ends with an exclamation mark. A command tells someone to do something; it has a bossy verb (an imperative verb) and ends with a full stop or an exclamation mark. The end mark alone does not tell you the type: Sit down! is a command.

kid: Sentences have jobs. A statement tells. My bike is red. A question asks. Where is my hat? It ends with a question mark.
An exclamation shows a big feeling. It starts with What or How. What a big dog that is! How tall you are! It ends with !
A command tells you what to do. It has a bossy verb. Shut the door. Stir the soup. The bossy verb is the doing word.
Look at the job, not just the mark. Sit down! ends with !, but it is bossy. So it is a command. To ask, move the verb to the front. The dog is hungry. Is the dog hungry?
adult: The English national curriculum for Year 2 asks children to learn how the grammar of a sentence shows its function as a statement, question, exclamation or command. US Common Core L.1.1j asks first graders to produce declarative, interrogative, imperative and exclamatory sentences. These are the same four types with formal names.

Each type has a form as well as a job. A question either starts with a question word or puts the verb before the subject: you can swim becomes can you swim. A command uses the imperative form of the verb with no subject, as in wash your hands. In the curriculum, an exclamation starts with What or How and contains a verb: what a big dog that is.

Common mistakes: deciding the type from the end mark alone, so Sit down! is called an exclamation; thinking the first word of a command is always the bossy verb, when Please or Carefully can come first; calling How tall you are! a question because it starts with How; and ending a question with a full stop. Be careful that one-word shouts such as Wow! are not full exclamation sentences.

In the lab your child sorts sentences by their job, taps the bossy verb in commands, moves the verb to the front to turn a statement into a question, picks What or How to start an exclamation, and takes away you to turn a statement into a command.

familyTip: Play sentence jobs at dinner. Say a sentence such as 'Pass the peas.' or 'What a big plate that is!' and let your child shout its job: tells, asks, big feeling or bossy. Then swap roles.

visual.caption: What is each sentence's job? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: What a hot day it is!

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort sentences by job, find bossy verbs, turn statements into questions, start exclamations with What or How, and make commands.

practice.prompt: Four types of sentences: 'Sit down!' ends with an exclamation mark. Is it a statement, question, exclamation or command?
practice.hint: Look at its job, not only its end mark. Does it tell someone to do something?
practice.explain: Sit is a bossy verb telling someone what to do, so it is a command. A command can end with ! when it is said strongly.

practice.prompt: Ben wrote {q} questions and {s} statements. How many question marks did he need?
practice.hint: Only one type of sentence ends with a question mark.
practice.explain: Each question ends with a question mark, so he needs {q}. The {s} statements end with full stops.

practice.hint: A question asks. Where is the verb can?
practice.explain: Can you swim? puts the verb can first and ends with a question mark. You can swim. is a statement and Swim to the side. is a command.

practice.prompt: A page has {n} sentences. {e} are exclamations and the rest are commands. How many commands are there?
practice.hint: Take the exclamations away from all the sentences.
practice.explain: {n} take away {e} is {=n-e}, so there are {=n-e} commands on the page.

pool.prompt: In 'Please shut the door.' which word is the bossy verb?
pool.hint: The bossy verb is the doing word. What are you told to do?
pool.explain: You are told to shut the door, so shut is the bossy verb. Please is a polite word and door is a thing.

pool.prompt: What type of sentence is 'How kind you are!'?
pool.hint: Does it ask something, or show a big feeling?
pool.explain: It starts with How but does not ask anything. It shows a big feeling and ends with !, so it is an exclamation.

pool.prompt: Turn 'The cat is asleep.' into a question.
pool.hint: Move the verb is to the front, then change the end mark.
pool.explain: Moving is to the front and ending with a question mark makes Is the cat asleep? Just adding ? does not change the order.

pool.prompt: Mia wrote {s} statements and {c} commands. Each ends with a full stop. How many full stops did she write?
pool.hint: Statements and these commands both end with a full stop. Add them.
pool.explain: {s} + {c} = {=s+c} full stops, one at the end of each sentence.

pool.prompt: Which word can start an exclamation sentence?
pool.hint: Think of What a big dog that is!
pool.explain: An exclamation starts with What or How. Is and Can start questions, such as Is it big?

pool.prompt: What type of sentence is 'Wash your hands.'?
pool.hint: Does it tell you something, or tell you to do something?
pool.explain: Wash is a bossy verb telling you what to do, so it is a command, even though it ends with a full stop.

pool.prompt: Which mark should end 'Where is my coat'?
pool.hint: Where is a question word. What does the sentence do?
pool.explain: It asks something, so it is a question and ends with a question mark: Where is my coat?

pool.prompt: Make 'You close the gate.' into a command.
pool.hint: Take away the word that says who. What word comes first then?
pool.explain: Taking away You leaves the bossy verb first: Close the gate. That is a command.

pool.prompt: Zoe wrote {c} commands. Each command has one bossy verb. She adds {k} more commands. How many bossy verbs now?
pool.hint: Every command needs its own bossy verb. Add the commands together.
pool.explain: {c} + {k} = {=c+k} commands, and each has one bossy verb, so there are {=c+k} bossy verbs.
